items.explanation: The author argues that attention has been retrained by an environment offering constant novelty and feedback, while books demand delayed reward and trust. The passage explicitly rejects a biological decline and notes that students can sustain attention on games and podcasts. The other options overstate the claim or invent a prescription the author never makes.
options: People have lost the biological capacity to concentrate on long texts.
Deep reading is threatened not by a loss of ability but by an environment that rewards distraction.
Digital media has made all forms of reading obsolete.
Universities should ban screens to restore deep reading.
items.passage: For most of human history, reading was a slow and demanding act. A reader of a long novel or a dense philosophical treatise had to hold several threads in mind at once, return to earlier passages, and tolerate long stretches in which nothing spectacular happened. The reward was not speed but depth: an intimacy with an argument that could only be earned by staying with it. In the last two decades, however, the conditions under which most reading takes place have changed so completely that the activity itself may have changed with them. Screens deliver text in fragments, interrupted by notifications, hyperlinks and the constant promise of something newer a swipe away. The question is not whether people still read, because they read more words than ever before, but whether the kind of reading that builds sustained attention is quietly disappearing. The evidence is mixed, and it is worth resisting both panic and complacency. Studies of university students show that many now report difficulty finishing a single long article without checking another application, yet the same students can spend hours immersed in a complex video game or a long-form podcast. Attention, it seems, has not vanished; it has been retrained. It follows novelty, interactivity and immediate feedback, and it withdraws from forms that offer none of these. This suggests that the problem is not a biological decline in the capacity to concentrate but a change in the environment that rewards concentration. A book, unlike a feed, does not reward the reader every few seconds. It asks for trust, the belief that the effort invested in the early pages will be repaid later, and such trust is hard to sustain when every competing medium offers repayment at once. None of this means that deep reading is doomed. Libraries, reading groups and the stubborn popularity of long novels suggest a continuing appetite for it. What is at stake is whether the institutions that once protected slow reading, schools, libraries and the unhurried evening, will continue to do so when the economics of attention push so strongly in the other direction. If they do not, we may keep the skill of decoding words while losing the habit of following a long thought to its end. That loss would be subtle, because we would still call what we do reading, but it would change what reading can do for us, and what kinds of ideas can survive in a culture that no longer pauses long enough to meet them.

items.explanation: The final paragraph explicitly calls the square a test of whether a city believes public life is worth paying for. The author concedes private management can have merits and public authorities can fail, so the passage is not a blanket condemnation. Nostalgia is not the framing; the argument is about present choices.
options: an example of failed urban planning.
a test of whether a city values shared public life.
proof that private management always fails.
a nostalgic memory of a lost past.
items.passage: The public square has always been an awkward piece of property. It belongs to everyone and therefore to no one in particular, which is precisely why it matters. In a square, a street vendor, a student, a pensioner and a chief executive occupy the same ground on the same terms, and that equality, however brief, is a political achievement. Yet across many cities, squares, parks and waterfronts are being redesigned, fenced, ticketed or handed to private managers who promise cleaner paving and better security. The bargain is presented as common sense: public money is scarce, private management is efficient, and a well-kept space benefits all. The difficulty is that efficiency and openness do not always point in the same direction. A privately managed square can be kept spotless by removing the people who make it untidy, the homeless person sleeping on a bench, the teenagers gathering after school, the protestors with their placards. Each removal can be justified on its own, as a matter of safety or order, but together they change the character of the place. It ceases to be a commons and becomes a curated amenity, pleasant for those who fit its intended use and unwelcoming to those who do not. Defenders of privatisation reply that a space nobody uses because it feels unsafe is no commons at all, and they have a point. A square overrun by crime or neglect serves no one, and public authorities have often failed to maintain the spaces in their care. The choice, however, is not between neglect and exclusion. Cities that have kept their squares genuinely public have usually done so by investing in maintenance, lighting and programming that invites many kinds of use at once, rather than by surrendering control to whoever can pay for the upkeep. The deeper question is what a city is for. If a city is only a machine for commerce, then its squares should be optimised like shopping malls. If it is also a place where strangers learn to share ground, then some inefficiency is the price of that lesson, and some spaces must remain open even to those who contribute nothing to their upkeep. The square, in this sense, is a test. A city that cannot tolerate an unprofitable bench has probably stopped believing that public life is worth paying for, and that disbelief, once it takes hold, is far more expensive than any maintenance bill.

items.explanation: The author stresses that tools have always shaped creative work and that the meaningful question is where human judgement is exercised, not whether a tool was used. Treating tool use as automatic disqualification would also condemn photography, printing and synthesisers. The passage never claims AI output is currently equal or that copyright is irrelevant.
options: Every artwork that uses a tool is less original.
The question should be where human judgement is exercised, not whether a tool was used.
AI-generated work can never be art.
Copyright law has already solved the problem of AI art.
items.passage: When the first photographs were exhibited, painters complained that a machine had stolen their craft. When synthesisers arrived, musicians were told that real instruments were dying. Each new tool has provoked the same anxiety, and each time the anxiety has proved partly right and mostly misplaced. The tool did change what artists could do, and it did make some skills less valuable, but it did not abolish art. It moved the interesting decisions elsewhere. That history is worth remembering as machines begin to generate images, music and text that are, at first glance, hard to distinguish from human work. The usual objection is that a machine cannot intend anything, and therefore its output cannot mean anything. There is force in this, but it proves less than it seems. Meaning in art has never depended solely on the intentions of the maker. A photograph can move us without the camera intending anything, and a reader can find significance in a poem that its author never planned. What matters is not whether a machine had intentions but whether a human being has made choices that matter: selecting, editing, arranging, rejecting and presenting. A person who generates a hundred images, discards ninety-nine, crops one and hangs it in a gallery has exercised judgement at every step, even if no brush touched the canvas. To deny that this is creative work is to insist that creativity lives only in the hand, not in the eye or the mind. None of this settles the harder questions. Who owns an image trained on the work of living artists, and who should be paid when that work is used? How should audiences be told that what they are seeing was machine-made? These are questions of fairness and honesty, not of metaphysics, and they deserve answers in law and in practice. But they should not be confused with the question of whether machine-assisted art can be genuine. It can be, just as photography could be, and the test is the same as it has always been: does the work reward attention, does it say something that could not be said more simply, and does it bear the mark of choices someone cared about? If it does, the machine that helped make it is no more a disqualification than the camera was, and no less a responsibility.

items.explanation: The passage says standard time made timetables, contracts and coordination possible, and that it also imposed a single rhythm on varied local lives. The author treats it as a powerful tool with real costs, not as a neutral technical fix or a purely harmful imposition. Local time was displaced, not preserved.
options: Standard time was a purely technical improvement with no social cost.
It was a powerful coordinating tool that also imposed one rhythm on varied local lives.
Local timekeeping was preserved alongside it.
It had no effect on how people experienced the day.
items.passage: Before railways, every town kept its own time. Noon was when the sun stood highest over that particular place, and a traveller moving twenty miles might find the clocks disagreeing by several minutes. This was not a problem until it became one, because most people rarely travelled far and had little need to coordinate with strangers. The railway changed that. A timetable cannot tolerate a different noon in every town, and so the companies imposed standard time, first along their lines and then, gradually, across whole nations. The change was presented as a matter of convenience, and in many ways it was. Trains could run to a schedule, contracts could specify hours, and strangers could agree to meet at three o'clock without first asking whose three o'clock they meant. Yet standard time was also a quiet revolution in how people experienced the day. Work began and ended at the same hour regardless of season, light or local custom. The body was asked to follow the clock rather than the sun, and the day was divided into uniform units that could be bought, sold and accounted for. This was enormously productive, and it was also, for many, a loss. Farmers, whose work had followed the seasons, found themselves yoked to a rhythm that ignored them. Religious observances tied to dawn and dusk had to be translated into clock time. Even leisure was reshaped: the evening became a slot between the end of work and bedtime, rather than the long, variable darkness it had been. None of this means that standard time should be abandoned. A modern economy cannot function without it, and the coordination it makes possible has brought real benefits, from safer travel to reliable communication. But it is worth remembering that the clock on the wall is not a fact of nature. It is an agreement, and like all agreements it serves some interests better than others. When we complain that there is never enough time, we may be complaining not about the hours themselves but about a system that treats every hour as identical and every minute as a unit to be spent efficiently. The question is not whether to keep standard time but whether we can remember, within it, that human lives do not run at a uniform speed, and that a timetable, however useful, is a poor description of a day well lived.

CBDA
BDCA

items.question: The sentences below, labelled A to D, form a coherent paragraph when arranged in the right order. Choose the correct order. A: Yet the most durable legacy of the project was not the bridge itself but the engineering methods developed to build it. B: When the bridge was proposed, critics called it impossible: the river was too wide, the winds too strong, the budget too small. C: The engineers answered by designing a new kind of cable that could be spun in place, rather than hauled across in sections. D: Construction took nine years, and on the day it opened, ten thousand people crossed it on foot.

BADC
DBAC

B: A seed bank is, in effect, a library in which the books are living things. C: If a crop fails or a variety disappears from the fields, its seeds can be withdrawn and grown again. D: The vault in the Arctic holds duplicates from collections all over the world.

ABCD

B: Their charts showed coastlines they had never seen, drawn from guesswork and the reports of others. C: The invention of an accurate way to measure longitude finally made those charts reliable. D: Today, a map is expected to be exact to the metre, a standard no early sailor could have imagined.

items.explanation: The paragraph balances flexibility against blurred boundaries and concludes that deliberate norms decide success, not location. The correct summary preserves both sides and the conditional conclusion. The other options claim only benefits, only harms, or a universal verdict the paragraph never gives.
options: Remote work is clearly better than office work in every respect.
Remote work has improved flexibility but blurred boundaries, so its success depends on deliberate norms rather than location alone.
Remote work has failed because employees cannot be trusted.
Office work should be abolished because remote work is always superior.
items.question: Choose the best summary of this paragraph. Remote work has given many employees control over when and where they work, and surveys repeatedly show that they value that freedom. Yet the same freedom has blurred the line between work and home: emails arrive at midnight, meetings multiply, and the working day stretches without a clear end. Companies that have managed the shift well have done so not by choosing a location but by setting norms, agreed hours, protected time off, and clear expectations about response times.

items.explanation: The paragraph says digitisation widens access and also says the physical encounter cannot be replaced, so the two claims must appear together. The correct option keeps digitisation as a complement. Options claiming replacement, uselessness or total superiority drop one side of the argument.
options: Museums should stop digitising their collections.
Digital copies are identical to seeing the original object.
Digitisation widens access but cannot replace the physical encounter, so museums should treat it as a complement, not a substitute.
Only famous museums benefit from digitisation.
items.question: Choose the best summary of this paragraph. Museums that put their collections online report a sharp rise in visitors who first encounter an object on a screen and later travel to see it in person. Digitisation also lets scholars compare objects held in different countries without travelling. Even so, curators insist that a photograph cannot reproduce scale, texture or the feeling of standing before the object itself, and that the screen is best used to invite people in rather than to keep them away.

items.explanation: After a 20 percent increase, the price is 120 percent of 100, or Rs 120. A further 10 percent discount is taken on 120, giving 108. Applying the discount to the original price would wrongly give 110.
items.question: The price of an item is Rs 100. It is increased by 20% and then discounted by 10%. What is the final price?

items.explanation: In 2.5 hours at 60 km per hour, the distance covered is 150 km. The remaining distance is 300 minus 150, or 150 km, to be covered in 1.5 hours, requiring 100 km per hour. The average speed for the whole trip is 75, which is not the required speed for the remainder.
items.question: A car must cover 300 km in 4 hours. It covers the first 2.5 hours at 60 km/h. At what speed must it travel for the remaining time?

items.explanation: There are 36 equally likely outcomes when two dice are rolled, and 6 of them sum to 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2) and (6,1). The probability is therefore 6 divided by 36, or 1/6. Counting only one ordering of each pair would halve the count.
items.question: Two dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is 7?

items.explanation: The sum of the first n natural numbers is n into (n plus 1) divided by 2. For n equal to 20, this is 20 into 21 divided by 2, or 210. Adding the terms one by one gives the same result but wastes time.
items.question: What is the sum of the first 20 natural numbers?

items.explanation: The area of a circle of radius 7 is pi into 49, which is 154 square units using pi as 22/7. The circumference would be 44, which is the trap option. Area uses the square of the radius.
items.question: What is the area of a circle of radius 7 units? (Use pi = 22/7)

items.explanation: Selling at Rs 1,200 after a 20 percent profit means the cost price is 1200 divided by 1.20, or Rs 1,000. Profit is therefore Rs 200. Subtracting 20 percent of the selling price would wrongly give 960.
items.question: An article is sold for Rs 1,200 at a profit of 20%. What is its cost price?

items.explanation: Downstream speed is 12 plus 4, or 16 km per hour, and upstream speed is 12 minus 4, or 8 km per hour. Time downstream is 24 divided by 16, or 1.5 hours, and upstream is 24 divided by 8, or 3 hours, totalling 4.5 hours. Using still-water speed for both legs ignores the current.
items.question: A boat's speed in still water is 12 km/h and the stream speed is 4 km/h. How long does it take to go 24 km downstream and return?

items.explanation: Let the father's age be 3x and the son's x; in 12 years their ratio is (3x+12) to (x+12) equal to 2 to 1. Solving gives x equal to 12, so the son is 12 now. The present ratio alone cannot fix the ages without the future condition.
items.question: A father's age is three times his son's age. In 12 years, the father's age will be twice the son's age. How old is the son now?

items.explanation: The equation x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0 factors as (x - 2)(x - 3) = 0, so the roots are 2 and 3. Their sum is 5, which also follows from Vieta's formula. The product of the roots is 6, not the sum.
items.question: If a and b are the roots of x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0, what is a + b?

items.explanation: The LCM of 12, 15 and 20 is found from prime factors: 12 is 2^2 into 3, 15 is 3 into 5, and 20 is 2^2 into 5. Taking the highest powers gives 4 into 3 into 5, or 60. The product of the three numbers is far larger and is not the LCM.
items.question: What is the LCM of 12, 15 and 20?

items.explanation: Simple interest is principal into rate into time divided by 100, which is 10000 into 6 into 2 divided by 100, or Rs 1,200. Compound interest would be slightly higher at Rs 1,236, so the two must not be confused.
items.question: What is the simple interest on Rs 10,000 at 6% per annum for 2 years?

items.explanation: Two-digit numbers whose digits sum to 7 are 16, 25, 34, 43, 52, 61 and 70. Of these, only 70 is divisible by 7, since 70 divided by 7 is 10. The other candidates fail the divisibility test, so 70 is the smallest such number.
items.question: What is the smallest two-digit number divisible by 7 whose digits sum to 7?

items.explanation: The volume of a cylinder is pi r squared h, which is (22/7) into 49 into 10, or 1,540 cubic units. The curved surface area would be 440, which is a different quantity. Volume uses the square of the radius and the height.
items.question: What is the volume of a cylinder of radius 7 units and height 10 units? (Use pi = 22/7)

items.explanation: The number of ways to choose 2 people out of 5 is 5C2, which is 10. Permutations would give 20, which counts order and overcounts for a committee. The combination formula divides by 2 factorial to remove ordering.
items.question: In how many ways can a committee of 2 be chosen from 5 people?
